analysis.one_liner: Cuts individual income tax to three flat rates of 10, 20, and 30 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 1999 with zero cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and died there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the individual income tax's five rates (15% up to 39.6%) with just three: 10%, 20%, and 30%. The bottom rate would drop from 15% to 10%, the middle 28% and 31% rates would collapse into 20%, and the top rate would fall from 39.6% to 30%. It would also cut the alternative minimum tax rates and lower a corporate surtax rate, effective in 2000 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who pays federal income tax would get a rate cut: a single worker earning $35,000 would see the 15% rate on all of that income drop to 10% [S3]. But the largest dollar gains would go to high earners, whose top rate falls 9.6 points (39.6% to 30%) and who would no longer face the 36% and 39.6% brackets at all, and to taxpayers subject to the alternative minimum tax, whose rates drop from 26% and 28% to 18% and 20% [S3]. Because most income is earned by high earners, most of the revenue cost flows from the cuts at the top [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the individual rate structure with three brackets — 10%, 20%, and 30% — so the bottom rate falls from 15% to 10% and the 28% and 31% middle rates become 20%, with the 20% bracket extending to $150,000 for joint filers and $125,000 for singles [S2][S3].
Cuts the alternative minimum tax rates from 26% and 28% to 18% and 20% [S2][S3].
Reduces the 39.6% top marginal rate to 30%, eliminating the 36% and 39.6% brackets entirely [S3].
Updates inflation-indexing baselines and cuts the 39.6% accumulated-earnings and personal-holding-company surtax rates to 30% [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury loses the revenue from the rate cuts, since the bill contains no offsetting tax increase or spending cut; that shortfall ultimately falls on everyone through a larger deficit or through cuts to federal programs. Within the tax code, the concentration of the loss is at the top — the 39.6%-to-30% top-rate cut costs the most revenue per dollar of income affected [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury, and everyone through deficits

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no offset to the revenue lost from the rate cuts; it simply cuts rates, so the full cost lands on the federal budget balance [S3].

The biggest dollar gains go to the highest earners: eliminating the 36% and 39.6% brackets cuts the top rate from 39.6% to 30%, while a $35,000 single filer's total gain is roughly $3,000 — much of the benefit relative to income rises with income [S3].

Trusts and estates keep their steep graduated rates (up to 39.6% above $8,450), so the flattening applies only to individuals and some corporations, complicating the code rather than simplifying it uniformly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a real rate cut to every income-tax payer — the bottom rate cut from 15% to 10% is proportionally large for low and moderate earners. But the design is a flattening of the rate structure whose largest dollar and revenue effects fall at the top and among AMT payers, and it pays for none of itself. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge the bill's cost is large and unoffset; an honest critic would note lower earners do come out ahead relative to their income.

outcome.mechanism: Frist introduced the bill, the Senate sent it straight to the Finance Committee, and no one ever brought it up again before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Frist introduced S. 1014, the '10-20-30 Act,' on May 11, 1999 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; that was its last recorded action [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor count stayed at zero for the bill's entire life [S4].
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, killing it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one: no taxpayer received the rate cut, and the Treasury avoided the bill's unoffset revenue loss.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; existing tax law stayed unchanged

for.name: Sen. Bill Frist
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 11, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: William V. Roth Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the committee took no action after it was referred on May 11, 1999.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no cosponsor of either party signed on, so no recorded positions exist beyond the sponsor's own.

industries.note: The top rate would fall from 39.6% to 30% and the AMT rates would drop, giving the largest dollar gains to the highest earners. Because the bill offsets none of that revenue, the cost falls on the public budget.
AMT rates would drop from 26% and 28% to 18% and 20%, a targeted benefit that mostly reaches upper-income filers, paid for by unoffset revenue loss.

industries.industry: Federal Treasury (public services and the deficit)
industries.note: The rate cuts across all brackets would reduce federal revenue with no offsetting provision, leaving a larger deficit or forcing cuts elsewhere that land on ordinary people.
